content: Choline is an organic compound that is classified as an essential nutrient and is often grouped with the Vitamin B complex. It is a natural amine that is present in the lipids that form cell membranes and in the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. The Food and Nutrition Board of the Institute of Medicine of the National Academy of Sciences has established adequate daily intake levels for choline, which range from 425 to 550 milligrams for adults. Choline was first discovered by Andreas Strecker in 1864 and was chemically synthesized in 1866. Chemically, choline is a quaternary saturated amine with the molecular formula (CH3)3N+CH2CH2OH X−, where X− represents a counterion such as chloride, hydroxide, or tartrate. Physiologically, choline and its metabolites serve three primary functions. First, they contribute to the structural integrity and signaling roles of cell membranes. Second, they are essential for cholinergic neurotransmission, as choline is a precursor for acetylcholine synthesis. Third, choline acts as a major source of methyl groups through its metabolite trimethylglycine (betaine), which participates in the synthesis of S-adenosylmethionine. When metabolized, choline can produce trimethylamine, a compound with a fishy odor. Consequently, excessive choline intake may result in a fishy body odor. Choline is also available as a dietary supplement. It is well-established that supplements of methyl group transfer vitamins, such as B6, B12, and folic acid, reduce blood homocysteine levels and help prevent heart disease. Choline is a critical source of methyl groups for these processes. Research by Central Soya scientists has shown that lecithin/choline supplements can reduce heart disease in laboratory studies. Choline supplements are sometimes marketed as smart drugs or nootropics due to the role of acetylcholine in various cognitive functions. Choline serves as a chemical precursor for acetylcholine, and studies suggest that memory, intelligence, and mood are partially mediated by acetylcholine metabolism in the brain. However, the efficacy, benefits, and potential side effects of choline supplementation remain subjects of ongoing debate. Research published in the New England Journal of Medicine has indicated that choline supplements may have adverse effects on individuals with clinical depression or bipolar disorder, as these individuals may be hypersensitive to acetylcholine. The FDA mandates that infant formula made from cow's milk must contain choline. Due to its role in lipid metabolism, choline is also included in some nutritional supplements that claim to reduce body fat. However, there is little to no evidence supporting the idea that choline reduces excess body fat or that high doses of choline increase fat metabolism. The richest dietary sources of phosphatidylcholine, the primary delivery form of choline, include egg yolks, soy, and cooked beef, chicken, veal, and turkey livers. Many foods contain trace amounts of free choline, even iceberg lettuce. The extent to which these trace forms are bioavailable to humans remains debated. In 2004, the USDA released its first database of choline content in common foods. The most commonly available choline dietary supplement is lecithin, which is derived from soy or egg yolks and is often used as a food additive. Phosphatidylcholine is also available as a supplement in pill or powder form. Choline is additionally available as choline chloride, which is a liquid due to its hydrophilic properties. Choline chloride is sometimes preferred as a supplement because phosphatidylcholine can cause gastrointestinal side effects.
